stemMd:
In paragraph 2, marked portion **[1]** reads:

> Okonjo learned the trade from her grandfather, a watchmaker who repaired instruments for the fishing **fleet, he never built a tide clock himself.**

Which choice makes the marked portion conform to the conventions of standard English?

options.label: A
options.textMd: fleet. He never built a tide clock himself.

options.label: B
options.textMd: fleet, he never built a tide clock himself.

options.label: C
options.textMd: fleet, he had never built a tide clock himself.

options.label: D
options.textMd: fleet, him never building a tide clock himself.

explanationMd:
Test each side of the comma to see whether it could stand alone as a sentence.

- "Okonjo learned the trade from her grandfather, a watchmaker who repaired instruments for the fishing fleet" — subject *Okonjo*, verb *learned*. A complete sentence.
- "he never built a tide clock himself" — subject *he*, verb *built*. Also a complete sentence.

Two complete sentences joined by nothing but a comma is a **comma splice**, and a comma is never strong enough to do that job. The available repairs are a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction such as *but*. Only the period appears among the choices.

Check your fix by reading the two new sentences separately and confirming each one is complete and says what the passage means: "Okonjo learned the trade from her grandfather, a watchmaker who repaired instruments for the fishing fleet." and "He never built a tide clock himself." Both stand up, and *he* still clearly refers to the grandfather.

Be careful not to be distracted by the long appositive, "a watchmaker who repaired instruments for the fishing fleet". It sits between the subject and the splice and makes the sentence look more complicated than it is; strip it out and the error is obvious.

distractorRationale.b: This is the passage as written, and it is the error itself: two independent clauses joined by a comma alone. Leaving the sentence unchanged leaves the comma splice in place.
distractorRationale.d: Replaces the subject pronoun *he* with the object form *him* and turns the verb into a participle, producing "him never building", which is not a standard English construction in this position and still leaves the comma doing work it cannot do.
distractorRationale.c: Changes the tense of the verb but not the punctuation. "He had never built a tide clock himself" is still an independent clause, so the comma splice survives untouched — a tense shift cannot repair a punctuation error.

accessibilityText: The tested sentence reads: "Okonjo learned the trade from her grandfather, a watchmaker who repaired instruments for the fishing fleet, he never built a tide clock himself." The four choices replace the words from "fleet" onward with: fleet, full stop, He never built a tide clock himself; fleet comma he never built a tide clock himself; fleet comma him never building a tide clock himself; and fleet comma he had never built a tide clock himself.

independentSolve.workingNotes: The original joins two independent clauses ('Okonjo learned...' and 'he never built...') with only a comma, a comma splice. Only (a) splits them with a period; (b) is the unchanged splice, (c) merely changes tense and keeps the splice, and (d) produces an ungrammatical absolute 'him never building'.

review.notes: Author solved the item and attempted to defend each distractor before keying it. Only one choice supplies end punctuation strong enough to separate two independent clauses; the option set deliberately contains no semicolon and no comma-plus-conjunction, so exactly one repair is available. Awaiting an independent blind solve. Options were reordered after review to remove answer-position bias; ids and labels were remapped with the key.
